content.content: Topic: why the number of subsets of an n-element set doubles each time n grows by one

summary:
Every finite set of n elements has exactly 2^n subsets, and the reason the count doubles each time n grows by one is a simple argument about choice. Consider a set with n elements and add one new element, call it x. Every subset of the new, larger set falls into exactly one of two groups. Either it leaves x out, or it contains x. The first group is precisely the subsets of the original n-element set, so there are as many of them as there were before. The second group is also in one-to-one correspondence with the old subsets: take any subset that contains x, remove x, and what remains is a subset of the original set. Going the other way, take any old subset and add x to it. Each old subset yields exactly one new subset with x, and each new subset with x yields exactly one old subset. So the two groups have equal size, and the total is twice the old count.

This is the whole mechanism. Adding an element doubles the number of subsets because every existing subset can be carried forward in two versions, one without the new element and one with it, and nothing else is possible. The count does not grow by adding some fixed amount. It grows by a factor, because the new element multiplies the choices rather than adding to them.

It helps to see why the count is 2^n in the first place. Build a subset by going through the elements one at a time and deciding, for each, whether it goes in or stays out. Each element offers two options, and the decisions are independent of one another. With n elements there are n such yes-or-no decisions, so the number of possible outcomes is 2 multiplied by itself n times, which is 2^n. Counting by a sequence of independent binary choices is the same idea as the doubling argument, seen from a different angle. The doubling argument shows that the count for n+1 is twice the count for n, and starting from 1 (the empty set, for n = 0) that recurrence gives 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on, which is exactly the powers of two.

Small cases make this concrete. The empty set has one subset, itself. A set {a} has two: the empty set and {a}. A set {a, b} has four: the empty set, {a}, {b} and {a, b}. Adding c gives eight, because each of those four subsets appears once without c and once with c: the four old ones, and the four old ones with c added. Writing them out shows the doubling directly, with no need for a formula.

The same reasoning explains why the number of subsets grows so quickly. A set of ten elements has 1,024 subsets, and a set of twenty has over a million. Each new element does not add one more subset; it doubles everything that already exists. This is why exhaustive search over all subsets of a set becomes infeasible so quickly, and why the power set is the natural object to think about when a problem involves choosing any combination of items.

The doubling view also clarifies a common confusion. People sometimes expect the number of subsets to grow like the number of elements, linearly, because each element is "one more thing." The subsets, though, are not a list of the elements; they are the combinations of elements, and every combination is available with and without each new item. Once that is clear, the exponential growth follows from the simple fact that each element is either present or absent, and that choice is made independently for every element in the set.

Adding c gives eight, because each of those four subsets appears once without c and once with c: the four old ones, and the four old ones with c added. Writing them out shows the doubling directly, with no need for a formula.
  
  The same reasoning explains why the number of subsets grows so quickly. A set of ten elements has 1,024 subsets, and a set of twenty has over a million. Each new element does not add one more subset; it doubles everything that already exists. This is why exhaustive search over all subsets of a set becomes infeasible so quickly, and why the power set is the natural object to think about when a problem involves choosing any combination of items.
  
  The doubling view also clarifies a common confusion. People sometimes expect the number of subsets to grow like the number of elements, linearly, because each element is "one more thing." The subsets, though, are not a list of the elements; they are the combinations of elements, and every combination is available with and without each new item.
